title: Chameleon and Early-Fusion Token-Only Multimodal Models

questions.question: What does early fusion change about how a transformer represents images and text?
options: Images are supplied only as labels for a text-only next-token model.
Images stay in a separate continuous tower until the final output layer.
Images become discrete tokens in a vocabulary shared with text.
Text is converted into image patches before entering the decoder.
questions.explanation: Early fusion quantizes image features into discrete IDs in the same vocabulary as text and modality markers, so one autoregressive decoder can read or emit both. A separate continuous vision tower joined late is the adapter design this approach contrasts with.

questions.question: A Chameleon VQ tokenizer maps an image feature map of 32x32 locations to one codebook index per location. How many image tokens result?
options: 1,024 tokens, from 32*32 locations.
32 tokens, from one token per row.
64 tokens, from 32 locations per axis added together.
8,192 tokens, one for each possible codebook entry.
questions.explanation: One codebook index is emitted for each spatial feature, so 32×32=1,024 positions produce 1,024 image tokens. The 8,192 value is the number of possible codebook IDs, not the number of spatial locations.

questions.question: How does the VQ-VAE choose a discrete image token for a continuous spatial feature?
options: Choose the codebook entry whose index matches the pixel row.
Take the mean of all codebook vectors and emit its coordinate.
Sample a random codebook vector and train a separate text label.
Select the nearest codebook vector by L2 distance and emit its index.
questions.explanation: For each continuous feature, vector quantization computes distance to learned codebook vectors and emits the closest entry’s integer index. Choosing a random entry would discard the feature information needed for reconstruction or prediction.

questions.question: What is a major training-stability role of QK-Norm in Chameleon's recipe?
options: Normalize image pixels after the VQ decoder has generated them.
Normalize query and key projections before their attention dot product.
Normalize the codebook index so all image tokens have the same ID.
Normalize the final text response after the decoder stops.
questions.explanation: QK-Norm applies LayerNorm to query and key projections before their dot product, controlling attention-logit scale and preventing magnitude explosion at depth. Normalizing image pixels or codebook IDs does not stabilize the attention calculation.

questions.question: A product must generate an image and then continue with text in one autoregressive response. Which design supports this directly?
options: A CLIP dual encoder that returns image-text similarity scores.
Late-fusion LLaVA with projected visual inputs and text-only output.
Early fusion with shared text and image tokens in one decoder vocabulary.
A Q-Former bridge whose only output is a text embedding.
questions.explanation: Because image and text tokens share one output vocabulary, Chameleon can emit an image-code sequence and then continue with text in the same autoregressive response. A text-only-output adapter VLM cannot generate image tokens this way.

questions.question: A deployment only needs image understanding and wants to reuse a strong pretrained LLM without an image-tokenizer quality ceiling. Which approach is the simpler fit?
options: An early-fusion Chameleon model that generates discrete image codes.
A shared vocabulary that requires generating an image for every prompt.
A late-fusion adapter VLM such as LLaVA or BLIP-2.
A VQ-VAE decoder trained to render images without an LLM.
questions.explanation: For understanding-only use, a late-fusion adapter can reuse a strong pretrained LLM and avoid making image generation depend on a discrete VQ reconstruction ceiling. Chameleon’s shared-token design is valuable when mixed-modality generation is required.
